STITCH: ROBUST APPEARANCE-INVARIANT VISUAL PLACE RECOGNITION FOR ANCHORING SOCIAL AR CONTENT IN THE REAL WORLD A DISSERTATION by PRONOB BHATTACHARJEE Enrollment No: 25565017 Mehta Family School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY ROORKEE ROORKEE – 247667, INDIA November, 2026 STITCH: ROBUST APPEARANCE-INVARIANT VISUAL PLACE RECOGNITION FOR ANCHORING SOCIAL AR CONTENT IN THE REAL WORLD A DISSERTATION Submitted in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the award of the degree of MASTER OF TECHNOLOGY in Artificial Intelligence by PRONOB BHATTACHARJEE Enrollment No: 25565017 Mehta Family School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY ROORKEE ROORKEE – 247667, INDIA November, 2026 © INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY ROORKEE, ROORKEE – 2026 ALL RIGHTS RESERVED Candidate’s Declaration I, PRONOB BHATTACHARJEE, present the dissertation entitled “Stitch: Robust Appearance-Invariant Visual Place Recognition for Anchoring Social AR Content in the Real World” in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the award of the degree of MASTER OF TECHNOLOGY in Artificial Intelligence, submitted to the Mehta Family School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee. The report documents the implementation, executed experiments and attributed prior research for the Stitch project, prepared under the guidance of Dr. R. Balasubramanian. All experimental results are linked to the accompanying commands, datasets and software artifacts. Published methods, public datasets and automated assistance are acknowledged in the report. This declaration is prepared for review and signature by the candidate. Balasubramanian and the Mehta Family School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, in the academic context of this report. The public Stitch repository, the authors of the cited methods, and the maintainers of the public datasets and research software are gratefully acknowledged. The report and presentation adopt the institutional artwork and layout references supplied by the author. The experiments, scripts and provenance records accompany the dissertation so that its claims can be reviewed and reproduced. Automated implementation and writing assistance formed part of artifact preparation; the author is responsible for reviewing the final submission. Personal acknowledgements may be added by the candidate before final submission. iv Abstract Stitch proposes a social augmented-reality interface in which digital posts are associated with phys- ical places and recovered when a later visitor observes the same scene. Its original implementation matches SIFT features to one reference image and projects content using a planar homography. This thesis investigates whether pretrained representations improve recognition and anchoring under appearance change while retaining a reproducible path toward mobile deployment. A modular implementation compares SIFT with FLANN, SuperPoint with LightGlue, CosPlace global retrieval, and a hierarchical combination of retrieval, local matching, geometric verification, and rendering. Experiments use a documented HPatches subset, a custom cross-time subset of real Tokyo 24/7 query photographs, and seeded photometric transformations of repository and benchmark images. Original scripts are executed through a bounded file-input adapter. All reported measurements, plots and tables are derived from preserved run outputs. The evaluation distinguishes retrieval, geometric acceptance and ground-truth homography accuracy. Tokyo metadata supports place labels but does not establish metric camera pose or planar anchoring error. Short contrastive adaptation trains only a projection head on disjoint HPatches places. Model export and integer quantization are tested using actual ONNX inference. The report documents accuracy losses, rejected anchors, and the limits of narrow galleries and synthetic illumination changes. The resulting artifact demonstrates a reproducible planar-AR research pipeline. It does not establish a city-scale AR cloud, a six-degree-of-freedom localization benchmark result, or phone- device performance. The deployment analysis specifies the mapping, calibration, tracking, privacy and evaluation work needed before persistent public AR content can be supported responsibly. v Contents Candidate’s Simultaneous localisation and mapping VPR Visual place recognition xxiii Chapter 1 Introduction 1.1 Motivation and application context Stitch begins with an application idea: a social feed whose organising surface is the physical world. A visitor could leave a photograph on a building facade, attach a note to a meeting point, or place a virtual object beside a familiar landmark. A subsequent visitor would recover that content by pointing a camera at the same scene. The repository describes this ambition through the metaphor of a social wall distributed across real surroundings [1]. This thesis uses “Facebook in the real world” as a motivating description, rather than as a statement of affiliation or of implemented social-network functionality. The idea creates a correspondence problem before it creates a graphics problem. The system must decide which stored place, if any, is visible. It must then determine how content associated with that place should project into the current camera image. A visually similar building is insufficient evidence for rendering a post on a particular window. Likewise, retrieving the correct street does not identify a stable coordinate frame for a three-dimensional object. Recognition and geometric alignment therefore require separate outputs and separate evaluation criteria. The original software provides a compact demonstration of this distinction. It detects SIFT features in a reference image and a camera frame, matches their descriptors, estimates a homography, and warps an overlay into the frame. The latest script adds optical-flow tracking and smoothing. These operations are useful for a locally planar target already represented by a reference photograph. They do not by themselves provide a place database, a city-scale search index, or a persistent world coordinate system. The engineering task is to extend that working demonstration while retaining its inspectable geometric basis. An appearance change challenges the first correspondence step. Daylight produces different shadows, contrast and visible detail from artificial illumination at night. Seasonal vegetation may remove or reveal structures. Weather can introduce reflections or reduce contrast. These changes interact with viewpoint: a correctly recognised scene may have little shared visible surface with the reference. Long-term visual-localisation benchmarks explicitly examine these difficulties [2]. A method suitable for Stitch must therefore be assessed on more than an unchanged photograph or a visually convincing overlay video. 1 Chapter 1. Introduction 1.2 Problem statement Let a place database contain reference images D = {I i }, place identifiers p i , and content records C p i . Given a query image I q , the system should return a place hypothesis, evidence supporting that hypothesis, a geometric transformation where identifiable, and the associated content. A rejection is a valid result when the evidence is inadequate. The planar research prototype studied here returns  b r→q , C , s , F(I q , D) = p b , H p b (1.1) where s contains diagnostic matching and verification information. When no candidate passes b are absent and no anchored content is rendered. verification, p b and H The desired invariance is conditional. A representation should ignore exposure and other nuisance changes while retaining evidence that distinguishes places. It cannot discard all local structure and still determine the intended surface. Nor can it restore image information destroyed by underexposure. “Appearance-invariant” in the project title therefore identifies the research objective; it does not claim mathematical invariance or universal robustness. The experiments measure how particular pretrained representations behave under documented changes. The resource constraint is also explicit. The available host is a laptop with an Apple M2 proces- sor and a limited-memory configuration, recorded in the environment artifact. The implementation uses CPU inference because the recorded runtime did not expose an available accelerator. A mobile-class design is investigated through compact descriptors, bounded feature counts, model export and quantization. A laptop CPU timing cannot establish performance on a phone, and the thesis does not make that substitution. 1.3 Objectives The first objective is a reproducible classical reference. The original scripts must be inspected and executed on their bundled video without requiring an unavailable private camera stream. A refactored implementation should retain the SIFT–FLANN–RANSAC structure while making image coordinates, failures and rendering masks explicit. This baseline anchors the discussion in measured behavior rather than an assumed weakness of handcrafted features. The second objective is a controlled comparison of learned components. SuperPoint with LightGlue supplies local correspondences; CosPlace supplies an image-level descriptor. Each has a different role. Their combination is evaluated alongside exhaustive local matching and global-only retrieval. Identical query lists and geometry settings are used within each protocol so that a benefit is not explained by an easier test subset or a more permissive RANSAC threshold. The third objective is to connect recognition to content. A place record must support reference photographs and posted assets, and a query must retrieve the content associated with its verified place. The implemented output is an image overlay attached to a reference-plane polygon. Video capture and rendering are included in the demonstration. The more ambitious multi-user service and three-dimensional anchor lifecycle are specified as architectural extensions, with implementation 2 Chapter 1. Introduction boundaries stated explicitly. The fourth objective is a thesis whose evidence can be audited. Raw predictions and pair statistics are retained. Plotting and table generation consume those files, and prose-level headline values use generated LaTeX macros. Dataset and checkpoint hashes identify the inputs. Commands and exit codes identify the actions that produced results, including failed download and environment checks. The report should make an unmeasured quantity visibly unavailable rather than filling a requested table with an invented estimate. 1.4 Research questions 1. Does pretrained local matching improve correspondence and accepted homography accuracy under the measured illumination and viewpoint changes? 2. How does global retrieval affect the candidate search needed for reliable place recognition, and when does its shortlist discard a geometrically useful reference? 3. How often does a plausible retrieval result lead to an accepted and correct place, and how does that differ from ground-truth planar alignment accuracy? 4. Does short contrastive adaptation of a compact projection head improve retrieval on held-out places and real cross-time images? 5. What accuracy, size and latency tradeoffs follow from an executed descriptor export and INT8 quantization attempt? Each question maps to an observable artifact. Pair statistics address the first; ranked predictions and candidate-count ablations address the second and third; the seeded training records address the fourth; native-versus-ONNX descriptors and timed inference address the fifth. Metric six- degree-of-freedom localization is excluded from these answers because the downloaded evaluation subsets do not supply the required calibrated poses and three-dimensional map. 1.5 Scope of the empirical contribution The public-data contribution comprises a deterministic HPatches subset and a custom Tokyo cross-time protocol. HPatches contributes real illumination and viewpoint changes with image-to- image homographies [3]. Tokyo contributes photographs captured at different times with place and orientation labels [4]. The latter protocol uses a small reference gallery drawn from the query collection; it is deliberately named a cross-time subset rather than the official Tokyo street-view retrieval benchmark. Its results support a narrow comparison under matched labels, not a claim of benchmark-leading performance. Synthetic queries serve a different purpose. They provide known geometric maps while varying brightness, gamma, colour balance, noise and contrast. Since all transformations are seeded, the same source identity can be followed through a controlled perturbation. However, altered 3 Chapter 1. Introduction pixels retain the original scene, visibility and much of its texture. Their performance is therefore interpreted as a stress test of an implementation, not as a substitute for real night imagery or evidence about winter conditions. The methodological contribution is the integration and evaluation of available pretrained components in the Stitch setting. No new foundation model, feature detector, or neural matcher is claimed. The short training experiment changes only a projection head on frozen global descriptors. Its purpose is to expose the practical consequences of limited adaptation data and descriptor compression. Treating a neutral or negative outcome as a valid answer is necessary to avoid selecting a favourable training seed after observing the test set. The software contribution includes modular extraction, matching, geometry, rendering, database and I/O modules; a command-line interface; configuration and tests; data/model acquisition scripts; evaluation and demonstration code; and a generated-report workflow. The reference database stores content alongside place identifiers so that the experiment exercises retrieval of an actual posted asset rather than merely drawing an arbitrary polygon after matching. Persisting that record on disk establishes local repeatability, while cross-device consistency remains future work. 1.6 Assumptions and boundaries The reference photograph is assumed to represent a surface on which a planar overlay is meaningful. Within that model, an estimated homography maps reference pixels to query pixels. A street scene is generally not planar, so an accepted Tokyo homography is evidence of a consistent image region, not proof that every part of the street obeys the same map. This distinction motivates the separate reporting of geometric acceptance and true homography success. The gallery is treated as known and locally available during the experiment. Reference descriptors and local features may be cached before a query arrives. Timings state whether they include this setup, image decoding, rendering and content-file access. The production design would need to constrain cache size and fetch latency. Those costs are analysed symbolically and through measured component sizes; they are not represented as measured cloud-service costs. The work assumes that dataset access does not imply unrestricted redistribution or commercial permission. Software and imagery have separate provenance. Official documentation is retained where available, and manual-fetch instructions identify larger benchmarks whose image and mapping archives were not downloaded. A future product must resolve additional content rights, user consent and location privacy before reusing a research pipeline in public spaces. 1.7 Organisation of the thesis Chapter 2 reviews the representations, geometric models, datasets and anchor services relevant to the project. Chapter 3 analyses the original scripts and their recorded execution. Chapter 4 describes the implemented modules and the proposed multi-user service boundary. Chapter 5 defines the downloaded subsets and all preparation rules. Chapter 6 develops the mathematical 4 Chapter 1. Introduction formulation and algorithms. Chapter 8 specifies hardware, metrics and experimental controls. Chapter 10 reports the measured comparisons and validity threats. Chapter 14 examines export, quantization and scaling. Chapter 17 treats privacy and abuse as system requirements. Chapter 18 answers the research questions and defines a staged roadmap. The appendices provide reproduction commands, directory structure, qualitative evidence and key source listings. The expanded technical treatment in Chapters 7, 9 and 11 derives coordinate transformations, separates decision metrics and traces stage-specific failures. Chapters 12 and 13 provides the complete scene-level evidence for every selected sequence and site. Chapters 15 and 16 documents executable verification contracts and a proposed revision-aware service design. Chapter E retains all oracle-pair outcomes, including failures. These additions expose more of the existing evidence without presenting it as a larger independently acquired experimental population. 5 Chapter 2 Background and Literature Review 2.1 Recognition, localisation and anchoring Visual place recognition asks which previously observed place is depicted in a query. Image retrieval implements this as ranking a gallery using visual descriptors. A retrieved image can supply an approximate location or a candidate region, but its similarity score does not determine the query camera’s geometric pose. Visual localisation instead estimates the camera transformation relative to a map. In a calibrated three-dimensional setting that transformation has rotation and translation components. The established long-term benchmark distinguishes retrieval-like recognition from six-degree-of-freedom localisation under changing conditions [2]. Anchoring adds an application coordinate convention. A post needs a position or surface in the map, and the current device needs a transformation from that map to its view. A planar reference image can provide such a convention for image overlays: content coordinates map to reference-image pixels and then to query-image pixels. General three-dimensional objects require a world or surface coordinate frame whose scale and orientation are known. These outputs impose different observability requirements and should not share a single undifferentiated “localisation success” score. This separation guides the experimental design. Global-only retrieval is evaluated as retrieval. A local matcher is evaluated on image pairs whose relationship is known independently. A complete candidate-search pipeline is evaluated both for its ranked place result and for whether its selected candidate passes verification. On HPatches, an additional ground-truth comparison checks the estimated mapping. This arrangement permits a matcher to be good even when retrieval misses its correct candidate, and permits a retrieval method to be good even when a query lacks enough shared surface for anchoring. 6 Chapter 2. Background and Literature Review 2.2 Handcrafted local features 2.2.1 SIFT SIFT constructs local descriptors around characteristic image structures selected across scale. Orientation assignment and gradient-distribution normalisation provide robustness to several nuisance transformations. Lowe’s account also makes clear that robustness is bounded: perspective distortion, severe appearance change and absent detail remain relevant [5]. Stitch uses the OpenCV implementation rather than reimplementing the detector. For this application, a local descriptor provides more than an image-level match. Each descriptor remains associated with a pixel location, so accepted correspondences constrain a geometric map. This is the central reason a global embedding cannot directly replace the original pipeline. The comparison tests whether learned keypoints and descriptors provide better correspondences while preserving that association. 2.2.2 Approximate matching and the ratio test FLANN selects approximate nearest neighbours using indexing strategies suited to descriptor search [6]. In the upstream scripts, a randomised tree index and a bounded search effort retrieve the first two neighbours for each reference descriptor. A ratio criterion rejects a match when its best neighbour is insufficiently separated from the second-best candidate. This ambiguity test is useful for repeated textures, although it cannot establish physical scene identity by itself. The implementation must also handle cases omitted by compact demonstrations. A query with no descriptors produces no candidate correspondences. A reference descriptor may receive fewer than two neighbours if the target set is too small. Neither condition should raise an unhandled tuple-unpacking error or lead to a reused anchor being interpreted as a new recognition. The refactor makes empty sets and rejection first-class outputs. 2.3 Learned local representations and matching 2.3.1 SuperPoint SuperPoint jointly predicts interest points and descriptors from an image. Its training framework uses synthetic supervision and homographic adaptation to improve repeatability without requiring manually annotated natural-image keypoints [7]. The present work uses publicly released pretrained weights. Neither the detector nor its descriptor backbone is trained on the evaluation subset. The practical hypothesis is that joint learning may preserve useful correspondence evidence when raw contrast or local gradient distributions change. That hypothesis remains empirical. The learned extractor can still miss features in severe low light, repeated patterns or regions with little texture. A bounded keypoint count is used for both local methods, so the learned method is not granted an unlimited correspondence budget. 7 Chapter 2. Background and Literature Review 2.3.2 SuperGlue and contextual assignment SuperGlue conditions correspondence decisions on both feature sets through a graph neural network with attention and a differentiable assignment formulation. It explicitly models unmatched features, allowing occlusion and non-repeatability to be handled within matching [8]. This provides the conceptual motivation for comparing a learned matching stage with nearest-neighbour filtering. SuperGlue itself is reviewed but not executed in this artifact. 2.3.3 LightGlue LightGlue revisits sparse learned matching with adaptive computation. Its official implementation supports SuperPoint and several other feature families and exposes mechanisms that adjust work to pair difficulty [9, 10]. The experiments use SuperPoint-compatible pretrained weights, CPU inference and the recorded confidence settings. Flash-attention acceleration is disabled so the tested execution path is explicit. Adaptivity matters for Stitch because a difficult night query may require more work than an easy repeated view. A single average latency can conceal that variation. The artifact consequently records per-pair times and separately profiles complete queries. However, a laptop inference result does not demonstrate the same adaptive performance in a mobile runtime: export operators, memory allocation and backend support must also be verified. 2.3.4 LoFTR and the detector-free alternative LoFTR establishes correspondences through coarse-to-fine dense feature interaction rather than relying on a separately detected sparse keypoint set [11]. Its larger contextual field motivates it as an alternative when repeated keypoints are scarce. It is not included in the executed comparison, which focuses on a sparse pipeline compatible with cached per-reference features. A claim about LoFTR’s accuracy or mobile cost on these subsets would require an additional run. 2.4 Global descriptors for place retrieval 2.4.1 NetVLAD NetVLAD makes residual aggregation trainable and uses weak place supervision to learn image embeddings for retrieval [12]. Its broader lesson is that visual similarity can be learned from place relationships rather than from generic object categories alone. In Stitch, this role is coarse candidate selection; it reduces the number of local reference-query comparisons before geometric verification. 2.4.2 CosPlace CosPlace addresses large-scale visual geo-localisation through a classification-based training formu- lation and releases compact pretrained retrieval models [13, 14]. The artifact selects a ResNet18 8 Chapter 2. Background and Literature Review model with a 512-dimensional output. The choice provides a smaller encoder than the larger released backbones and a straightforward convolutional export path. It is an engineering selection for the available host, rather than a demonstrated optimum among all modern retrieval systems. 2.4.3 MixVPR and foundation features MixVPR aggregates feature maps through feature mixing and is a relevant alternative to residual aggregation [15]. DINOv2 provides self-supervised visual features that can also motivate retrieval pipelines [16]. These approaches are discussed to position the selected model within the literature. They are not silently substituted for CosPlace, and the thesis attributes no locally measured performance to them. 2.4.4 Candidate retrieval as a bottleneck If a correct reference is absent from the selected shortlist, a downstream matcher cannot recover it without expanding the search. A small shortlist can therefore improve latency while reducing the ceiling on successful anchoring. Increasing its size may recover relevant references but also adds expensive nonmatching pairs and more opportunities for a false geometric acceptance. The stage ablation varies shortlist size on exactly the same queries to expose this tradeoff. A retrieval score also has no universal probability interpretation. Cosine similarity measures proximity in the selected descriptor space. Its distribution changes with gallery composition, camera conditions and training domain. Treating a high similarity as permission to display content would bypass the local evidence needed to identify an anchoring surface. The no-geometry ablation is retained as a diagnostic, not as the recommended rendering policy. 2.5 Projective geometry and robust estimation Image correspondences constrain different geometric models depending on scene structure and calibration. Homographies describe plane-induced image mappings and pure-rotation cases. Essential matrices describe calibrated two-view epipolar relationships. PnP estimates camera pose from known three-dimensional points and their image projections [17, 18]. Stitch’s available assets and HPatches supply a direct planar formulation; the downloaded Tokyo metadata does not supply the calibrated 2D–3D relationships needed for PnP. RANSAC estimates a model from subsets of tentative correspondences while rejecting gross outliers [19]. It does not transform an inappropriate model into a physically correct one. A street scene may admit many correspondences on one facade while foreground objects remain inconsistent with the same homography. Similarly, repeated windows may support a projective map to the wrong location. Inlier support is therefore necessary evidence for this prototype, but it is not complete evidence of place identity or three-dimensional consistency. 9 Chapter 2. Background and Literature Review 2.6 Hierarchical visual localisation Coarse-to-fine localisation combines global hypotheses with local geometric evidence. HF-Net demonstrates this principle using jointly predicted local and global representations [20]. The present system adopts the hierarchy but uses separate pretrained networks and a planar verifier. Its proposed combination is an integration choice, not a claim to originate hierarchical localisation. Separating the stages remains valuable for a small research artifact. Each component can be replaced and each failure can be attributed to a recorded intermediate output. A wrong shortlist, an inadequate correspondence set and an inaccurate accepted homography become different diagnoses. The resulting modularity also exposes costs that a monolithic end-to-end timing would hide, such as reference extraction and content asset loading. 2.7 Benchmarks and domain coverage HPatches offers image sequences with illumination or viewpoint variation and known planar relationships [3, 21]. It is suited to evaluating image alignment, but it does not establish geographic recognition over a city or metric pose accuracy. A small distractor gallery assembled from its sequence references is an explicit custom retrieval task. Tokyo 24/7 was designed around changes in time of day and viewpoint, with camera-phone queries and a street-view database [4]. Using its accessible query photographs as both cross-time references and queries creates a useful paired recognition experiment but changes the task. The benchmark’s original database scale and ground-truth conventions must not be carried over to this subset’s results. Aachen Day-Night, RobotCar Seasons and Extended CMU Seasons extend evaluation toward long-term metric localisation [2, 22]. MSLS provides broader geographic, seasonal and sequence variation [23]. Those capabilities motivate future validation, while their absence from the executed image set limits what this thesis can conclude about seasonal robustness and map-level localisation. 2.8 Persistent AR services and lifecycle ARCore Cloud Anchors uses hosted scene information and an anchor identifier to support later resolution by devices observing the environment [24]. ARKit world maps support saving spatial state and attempting relocalisation in a later session [25]. These systems demonstrate that persis- tence involves mapping and coordinate recovery, not only content storage. Their documentation informs the proposed integration boundary; neither service is called by the experiments. Azure Spatial Anchors is relevant historically, but Microsoft states that the service was retired in November 2024 [26]. It is therefore discussed as background rather than recommended as a new dependency. This distinction illustrates why service status must be checked independently of the publication date of an AR architecture proposal. 10 Chapter 2. Background and Literature Review 2.9 Research gap addressed by the artifact The literature already provides strong representations, matchers and hierarchical localisation designs. The immediate gap in Stitch is the absence of an evaluated connection between those components and its reference-plane rendering demonstration. The artifact addresses that gap by preserving the classical behavior, introducing explicit place records, executing controlled comparisons, and making rejection and uncertainty visible. The remaining gap is larger: metric map construction, cross-device anchor management and realistic phone validation are still required for the original social-AR ambition. 11 Chapter 3 Analysis of the Existing System 3.1 Inspected source snapshot The upstream repository was cloned and inspected at the revision recorded in the bibliography and model/data provenance. Its executable Python content comprises tep.py, tep2.py and tep3.py. Bundled media include a reference image, a test image, an overlay, a short video and an animated walkthrough. No labelled place database, learning code or downloadable benchmark is included [1]. The original scripts remain present and unmodified in the working artifact. The inspection distinguishes what is implied by comments from what the code actually does. In particular, the latest script is not simply a frame-by-frame SIFT matcher: it includes optical flow, adaptive detection intervals, forward–backward checking and homography smoothing. Consequently, comparing its tracking speed directly with a learned re-recognition pass would confound different workloads. Both workloads are useful, but they answer different questions. 3.2 The file-processing script 3.2.1 Initialisation tep.py reads reference.jpg in grayscale and overlay.png in colour. It constructs a SIFT extractor with the upstream feature budget, extracts reference descriptors once, and resizes the overlay to the reference dimensions. A FLANN matcher uses the recorded tree and search settings. The input is video.mp4; the output writer uses a reduced playback frame rate. That output frame rate is a presentation choice and must not be interpreted as measured inference throughput. Reference caching is an important strength. It avoids repeating work that is unchanged across frames. The same principle is preserved in the modular system, where local reference features and global gallery descriptors are prepared before an online query. A fair runtime report must therefore state whether this preparation is included. The upstream bounded execution includes initialisation, whereas the later warm profiles isolate query-time processing. 12 Chapter 3. Analysis of the Existing System 3.2.2 Frame processing and verification Each frame is converted to grayscale, blurred and enhanced with CLAHE. SIFT descriptors are extracted from the enhanced image. The first two descriptor neighbours are compared with the script’s ratio threshold. A tentative homography is estimated only after enough matches survive; it is used only after an additional inlier-count test. These operations are conceptually sensible but encode thresholds and preprocessing directly in a monolithic script. The reference and query are not processed identically. The reference is loaded directly as grayscale, whereas the query receives blur and local contrast enhancement. This asymmetry is part of the preserved upstream behavior. The controlled A–D experiment instead uses a common image-resizing convention and shared geometry thresholds, with the difference documented. The latter is a normalised comparison of methods, not a claim of byte-for-byte reproduction of every upstream preprocessing decision. 3.2.3 Persistence and compositing When a new homography is unavailable, tep.py can reuse the previous one for a bounded number of frames. This can maintain visual continuity during a short detection failure. It can also display an old transformation after camera motion, because the reused map is not updated by a geometric motion model. A rendered frame is therefore not equivalent to a successful fresh recognition. The overlay mask is inferred from warped image intensity. Pixels that are sufficiently dark are treated as transparent. This is simple for demonstration assets, but it makes legitimate black content disappear and does not represent semi-transparency. The refactored renderer uses an explicit alpha plane and premultiplied colour. A unit test verifies that an opaque black overlay remains opaque and that a fully transparent one leaves the frame intact. 3.3 The first live-stream variant tep2.py follows the same broad matching and rendering sequence but reads a stream and displays a window. In the inspected snapshot, the example URL definition is commented out while the variable is subsequently used. Native execution therefore lacks a required input value. The script also continues when a frame read fails, without a finite retry policy or an EOF distinction. These issues are I/O failures rather than evidence about the SIFT algorithm. The execution adapter supplies a file source and suppresses display calls so that the vision code can be exercised in this environment. It does not invent a live phone experiment. The code path is labelled “bounded file-input adapter” in the result record, and the original stream requirement is retained in the source analysis. 13 Chapter 3. Analysis of the Existing System 3.4 The latest detection-and-tracking variant 3.4.1 Detection and scheduling tep3.py reads a hard-coded private DroidCam URL and resizes frames to a fixed working shape. During detection it downsamples the grayscale query, extracts SIFT descriptors, matches them to the full reference descriptors, and rescales matched query points back to working-frame coordinates. This coordinate correction is necessary: fitting the homography in a mixture of downsampled and full-frame pixels would corrupt the overlay location. Detection is attempted at an interval rather than on every frame. Failed detections increase that interval up to a cap. A successful detection resets the schedule and initialises tracking. This reduces repeated expensive searches when a target is absent, but it also introduces recognition delay. A frame-count average can look favourable partly because some frames perform little or no recognition work. The bounded execution therefore reports decoded frames, homography calls and warp calls separately. 3.4.2 Optical flow and consistency checks Once points are available, pyramidal Lucas–Kanade optical flow propagates their positions between frames. A periodic backward pass checks whether tracking approximately returns to the previous point positions. A geometric filter further rejects motions that differ substantially from median motion. These checks target local tracking errors; they do not compare a newly visible place with a database. The source contains implementation limitations worth preserving in the audit. It does not fully validate all optional optical-flow outputs before indexing them, and the backward-status array is not incorporated into every acceptance decision. A feature set may therefore be lost abruptly rather than producing a clean diagnostic rejection. The modular recognition path handles empty feature sets and model-estimation failures explicitly. It does not claim that every tracking behavior has been ported or improved. 3.4.3 Homography smoothing The tracking correspondences estimate a fresh homography. A determinant-based validity check rejects nonfinite or implausibly scaled matrices. The script may lock the prior transformation when average point motion is small, or blend matrix entries with the new estimate when motion is larger. This can reduce visible jitter in the demonstration. However, a homography is defined only up to scale. Entrywise averaging is not generally invariant to that representation, and a smooth matrix sequence need not correspond to the intended surface motion. The determinant is also affected by multiplying the whole matrix by a scalar. The new verifier normalises the matrix representation, checks rank and numerical conditioning, and examines the projected reference boundary. More principled temporal filtering in a calibrated pose or surface-coordinate space remains a deployment extension. 14 Chapter 3. Analysis of the Existing System 3.5 Execution protocol and measured baseline The three scripts were executed through scripts/run_originals.py. The adapter redirects video capture to the bundled file, supplies the missing URL variable where needed, suppresses GUI display, and terminates the run after the same decoded-frame budget. It wraps homography and warping calls to count them without changing their arguments or results. The exact command, elapsed time, exit state and raw output are preserved in the command journal. Table 3.1: Measured upstream-script execution on the same bounded file input. Timing includes initialization and file I/O. Script Frames H estimates Warps ms/frame tep.py tep2.py tep3.py 90 90 90 90 90 87 90 90 87 66.83 61.56 12.34 Table 3.1 reports the recorded measurements. The latest script’s lower average time is consistent with its design: many frames track an existing target rather than recomputing complete SIFT detection and matching. The earlier scripts repeatedly detect and describe features. The table cannot isolate an algorithmic speedup independent of this workload change, nor does it establish behavior on a real day/night stream. The bundled video provides a functional regression input. It tests decoding, feature processing, homography calls and output writing on the media supplied with the project. It lacks a ground-truth pose, framewise homography annotations and independent place labels. The number of nonnull estimates or warps therefore describes execution, not accuracy. Later benchmark experiments supply the missing ground-truth comparison where available. 3.6 Failure mechanisms motivating the redesign The first limitation is a fixed reference identity. Every successful match is interpreted relative to one target image. There is no mechanism to select among stored places or attach multiple users’ posts to a shared identity. Adding a gallery without explicit rejection would introduce false-place overlays, because even a nonmatching frame can have nearest neighbours. The second limitation is that temporal continuity is used to bridge a recognition failure. Reuse and tracking help when the correct target has already been found, but they do not solve re-entry under a different appearance. A visitor arriving at night needs a fresh correspondence to the stored representation. That task motivates the learned local and global components evaluated here. The third limitation is implicit state. Input configuration, recognition thresholds, cached geometry and rendering all live in script-level variables. A failure in one stage can be difficult to attribute. Separating extraction, matching, verification and compositing makes it possible to store the evidence supporting an anchor and to distinguish a wrong retrieval from a bad homography. The fourth limitation is the absence of experimental accounting. Without fixed query lists, 15 Chapter 3. Analysis of the Existing System ground truth, saved predictions and runtime definitions, a demonstration can support only a narrow claim that an overlay appeared on selected footage. The redesign adds this accounting before drawing broader conclusions. Its aim is to establish which parts of the original idea are supported by measured evidence and which remain a research or deployment requirement. 16 Chapter 4 System Design and Architecture 4.1 End-to-end responsibilities The implemented system divides a query into capture or decoding, preprocessing, place hypothesis generation, local correspondence, geometric verification, content lookup and rendering. The division follows the different evidence required at each stage. Capture supplies pixels; retrieval supplies candidate identities; geometry supplies a mapping; the database supplies content associated with the verified identity. A later stage is not allowed to turn an absent earlier result into an apparently successful anchor. File, video or camera decode and resize CosPlace descriptor candidate retrieval SuperPoint features LightGlue matches Reference- plane warp alpha com- positing Verified place ID content records RANSAC homography accept or reject On-disk place database: references, descriptor index, posted assets and normalised anchor polygons Figure 4.1: Implemented hierarchical recognition and planar content-rendering flow. The diagram is an architectural specification, not a measured throughput result. Figure 4.1 depicts the implemented path. The classical mode replaces the global shortlist and learned correspondence stage with exhaustive SIFT–FLANN verification. The learned-local mode removes global retrieval but retains exhaustive SuperPoint–LightGlue comparisons. Keeping those alternatives behind the same query interface makes stage removal explicit rather than changing the application data model for each method. 17 Chapter 4. System Design and Architecture 4.2 Module contracts 4.2.1 Image I/O and coordinates The I/O module returns a decoded BGR image and the transformation from original image coordinates to the working resolution. This second output is essential for evaluation: ground-truth homographies are expressed in the original images, whereas inference uses resized images. The module preserves aspect ratio and records separate horizontal and vertical scale values after integer rounding. It rejects unreadable files instead of returning an empty array that fails later in feature extraction. The video iterator accepts a file path, numeric webcam index or stream URL. It stops on EOF or a failed read and releases the capture resource. An explicit frame limit supports bounded experiments. A production live-stream client could add a retry state with a deadline; that policy should be kept outside geometry and should not silently reuse the last camera frame as a new observation. 4.2.2 Local features and correspondences A local-feature record contains pixel coordinates, descriptor arrays and any model-specific tensors required by the matcher. The shared interface returns two coordinate arrays and the descriptor- index pairs that produced them. Empty output has a stable shape. This allows geometry to reject insufficient support without depending on the internal format of either OpenCV or LightGlue. Learned features are associated with the resized image, and internal extractor resizing is disabled for the controlled comparison. Reference features are cached when the pipeline is constructed. Query features are extracted once and reused across candidates. This division avoids measuring repeated extraction merely because a shortlist contains several references. 4.2.3 Geometry and verification The geometry module returns the estimated homography, an inlier mask, count and ratio, and a separate acceptance flag. Retaining a rejected matrix for diagnostics is useful, but rendering checks the acceptance decision through the pipeline’s selected prediction. A matrix existing in memory does not itself authorise an overlay. The interface also exposes corner projection and camera-pose error utilities for tests and future calibrated evaluations. The acceptance policy combines sufficient correspondence support with numerical and boundary checks. This policy is common to the normalised local-method comparison. It is intentionally distinct from the original scripts’ hard-coded thresholds, whose unmodified results are reported separately. The distinction prevents a software refactor from being mistaken for a perfectly controlled reproduction of every upstream heuristic. 18 Chapter 4. System Design and Architecture 4.2.4 Global retrieval The global module loads the official CosPlace weights into the compatible ResNet18 and pooling architecture. Random ImageNet initialisation weights are not downloaded because the complete pretrained state is supplied by the selected checkpoint. A fixed preprocessing path resizes to the recorded descriptor input shape and applies channel normalisation. Gallery and query descriptors follow the same path. Ranking uses the dot product of normalised vectors with stable tie ordering. Exact search is appropriate for the small galleries in this artifact and makes the evaluation easy to inspect. An approximate index would introduce another source of candidate recall loss; it should be evaluated separately before a larger deployment. The descriptor index stores image fingerprints so stale references cannot be silently matched against an obsolete cached vector. 4.3 Place-database schema The database document has a schema version and a list of places. Each place has a unique identifier, one or more reference-image paths, and a list of posted-content records. Paths resolve relative to the database document so the artifact can be moved as a directory. The schema keeps a place identity distinct from a particular reference view: adding a second photograph need not duplicate all associated posts. Listing 4.1: Implemented place-record structure with illustrative identifiers. The numerical anchor coordinates are configuration values, not experimental results. { "schema_version": 1, "places": [{ "id": "place_identifier", "references": ["reference_view.jpg"], "content": [{ "id": "post_identifier", "kind": "image", "asset": "posted_image.png", "author": "example-user", "created_at": "2026-11-05", "anchor_normalized": [ [0.2, 0.2], [0.8, 0.2], [0.8, 0.65], [0.2, 0.65] ], "opacity": 0.8 }] }] } Listing 4.1 shows the implemented fields. Normalised polygon coordinates preserve the intended reference region when an image is resized. They describe a quadrilateral in the reference image, not a metric plane pose or a three-dimensional volume. The asset can retain its own alpha channel. The current renderer consumes image assets; the schema’s content-kind field provides a point for future video, note and mesh renderers without claiming they are implemented. The index is stored in a companion compressed NumPy file. It contains descriptors, reference 19 Chapter 4. System Design and Architecture paths, image hashes, the encoder checkpoint hash and preprocessing settings, including the image resize limit. Loading checks the index version, reference list, fingerprint count, configuration and finite descriptor matrix. A changed reference image, checkpoint or resize limit requires rebuilding. Enforcing cache-size limits remains a service implementation requirement. Each content polygon is associated with one reference photograph. An optional reference field selects that photograph; when omitted, the first reference is used. A post is rendered only through its associated reference. Adding a second photograph does not transfer polygon coordinates between views; that requires a validated geometric relation. 4.4 Implemented query behavior A query extracts its local features once. In full mode it also extracts a global descriptor and ranks references, selecting the configured shortlist. Each candidate receives local matching and RANSAC verification. Accepted candidates are ranked by inlier count and then inlier ratio. If none is accepted, the returned place identifier is absent. Otherwise, the selected reference and the content records belonging to that reference’s place are returned together. Rendering loads each selected asset, maps its corners to its reference-anchor polygon, composes that map with the reference-to-query homography, and alpha-composites into the query frame. This implements a complete local recognition-to-content path. The content is not selected by manually choosing an overlay after observing a query result. It is retrieved through the matched place record. Candidate diagnostics accompany the decision. They record place identifiers, support counts, ratios and acceptance flags. These diagnostics make it possible to explain why a familiar scene did not display a post: the correct reference may be outside the shortlist, or its local support may be inadequate. A user interface could convert those states into a prompt to move the camera or improve lighting. The research CLI reports the evidence directly. 4.5 Proposed multi-user posting and retrieval flow Design scope. The following specification describes an engineering extension; it is not a claim that a deployed multi-user service was measured. A production posting transaction would begin with an authenticated user observing an already mapped place or requesting creation of a new place. The client would submit a reference observation and a proposed anchor. A server would validate the observation, associate it with a map revision and persist the content record only after the identity and permissions are established. An unresolved observation should remain a draft rather than create a potentially incorrect public anchor. A later visitor would first obtain nearby place candidates, using an approximate location prior if the user permits it. Visual retrieval and geometric verification would establish a local map relation. The service would then return only content visible to that visitor under access and moderation rules. Content delivery and anchor resolution are separate operations: resolving a 20 Chapter 4. System Design and Architecture place must not expose a private post merely because its author once used that map. Posting client observation + draft propose Place/map Content service verified ID service permissions verify + version + assets query Visiting client recognise + resolve authorised content Figure 4.2: Proposed multi-user service responsibilities. These network transactions are not implemented or load-tested in the local artifact. Figure 4.2 separates the responsibilities needed to make the original social concept credible. A map service controls coordinate consistency and reference revisions. A content service controls visibility, asset retrieval and moderation state. The client controls capture, local inference and presentation. This division prevents an image-matching success from being overloaded as proof of authorisation, current map validity and safe content. 4.6 API and consistency sketch An API could expose a place-creation operation, an observation-verification operation, content posting, content retrieval and anchor retirement. Each response should include a place ID and map revision, not only a raw pose or homography. Posting should be idempotent under a client- generated request key so a network retry cannot create duplicate objects. Updating a map should create a new revision and retain an explicit relation to existing anchors. Anchor migration is a geometric operation. If an old reference plane is replaced, old polygon coordinates cannot simply be copied into an unrelated photograph. The service would need a validated transformation or a human-assisted reattachment. Until that relation exists, affected posts should be marked unresolved. This policy is more defensible than rendering an obsolete anchor with a stale cached homography. Content deletion should remove the public record and invalidate cached asset access, while map deletion should address references and derived indexes. An audit record may retain a minimal event description without retaining the original image indefinitely. These design choices are discussed as requirements rather than as implemented guarantees. The local database is intentionally small and file-based, which supports inspection but does not provide concurrent transactions or distributed deletion. 4.7 Server and device allocation The implemented artifact runs entirely on the host CPU. For a mobile deployment, global retrieval could remain on device for a geographically limited gallery, while a server supplies additional map 21 Chapter 4. System Design and Architecture candidates. Local verification could also run on device after downloading sparse reference features. The tradeoff depends on model size, bandwidth, privacy requirements and the measured phone execution backend; those quantities cannot be decided from desktop throughput alone. A viable interaction loop should separate occasional recognition from high-frequency tracking. The original tep3.py already illustrates this principle for a known target. Learned recognition could establish or refresh the map relation, after which the native AR tracking system updates the view. This architecture would not require executing the full hierarchical recogniser at the display refresh rate. Nevertheless, tracking drift and recovery latency would need their own measurements before the system could be described as persistent. 4.8 Testability and failure containment The module boundaries support tests with known transforms and synthetic outliers, independently of network downloads. The database can be inspected without loading a neural model. Rendering can be tested with an opaque black asset and a transparent asset. I/O failures can be reproduced through bounded files. These checks protect coordinate and state conventions that otherwise produce convincing but incorrect overlays. The main containment rule is rejection on insufficient evidence. A missing descriptor set, failed estimate, singular transform or absent verified candidate returns no anchor. Qualitative demonstrations retain these failures visibly. The resulting behavior may display less content than a permissive prototype, but it provides an interpretable basis for studying whether a future recognition improvement actually increases correctly supported anchors. 22 Chapter 5 Datasets and Data Preparation 5.1 Selection principles and evidence levels The repository contains demonstration media but no labelled research dataset. Data acquisition was therefore part of the experiment. Selection prioritised reachable public files, variation relevant to the application, ground truth appropriate to the measured task, and a subset size compatible with the available host. Two complementary public collections were selected: HPatches for planar geometric evaluation and Tokyo query photographs for real cross-time place recognition. A generated set adds controlled photometric perturbations. These collections supply different evidence levels. A labelled place identity establishes whether a retrieved record refers to the intended location. A homography establishes a planar pixel mapping. A calibrated camera pose and three-dimensional map would establish metric localisation error. The first two are present in the selected data; the third is not. The report does not infer missing ground truth from visual plausibility, GPS labels or a fitted matrix. Table 5.1: Downloaded and generated evaluation collections. Datasets and Data Preparation 5.2 HPatches subset 5.2.1 Acquisition and deterministic selection The original HPatches host failed DNS resolution during the recorded download check. The dataset author’s Hugging Face mirror was reachable and supplied the full sequence archive. The manifest records its URL, file hash, extracted-image hashes and per-sequence file counts. This distinguishes a verified local copy from a statement that a URL happened to exist when the thesis was written. The selected evaluation set consists of the first twelve sequence names in lexicographic order for each of the illumination and viewpoint prefixes. Every selected sequence contributes its reference image, all five targets and their corresponding homography files. Thus 144 images and 120 reference-target pairs are evaluated. The choice uses names and metadata before inference, rather than selecting pairs on which one method appears stronger. The images are resized only when loaded by the common I/O module. Original homographies remain unmodified on disk. Their transformation into the working-image coordinate convention is computed during evaluation. This avoids creating a second ambiguous ground-truth directory whose matrices might no longer correspond to the original files. The exact selected names are listed in Chapter B. 5.2.2 Illumination and viewpoint protocols The two prefix groups are evaluated separately because they probe different failure mechanisms. Illumination sequences change the appearance of a scene while retaining a related view. Viewpoint sequences change the projective relationship and visible detail. The official dataset description motivates this distinction [3, 21]. No attempt is made to relabel every illumination pair as a day/night pair: the prefix is the authoritative task label available for this experiment. For matching, each target is paired with its own sequence reference. For the custom retrieval task, the gallery contains one reference from every selected sequence, and a target’s correct identity is its sequence name. This provides distractors and a reproducible image-retrieval exercise. It does not add geographic coverage or convert HPatches into a city-scale VPR benchmark. Related targets from one sequence also remain statistically dependent, which motivates clustered uncertainty estimates. 5.2.3 Rights and source attribution HPatches combines sequences with source-specific attribution described by its maintainers. The repository’s software license should not be assumed to grant a blanket commercial license for all imagery. The artifact retains source links and uses the data as a research input. Any distribution of extracted photographs or a public product built from them requires review of the original source terms. This limitation is documented rather than replaced with an unsupported “open data” label. 24 Chapter 5. Datasets and Data Preparation 5.3 Tokyo cross-time subset 5.3.1 Available archive and labels The accessible Tokyo archive contains camera-phone query images and CSV metadata. The metadata identifies image filenames, geographic positions, viewing-direction labels and capture- condition labels. The original dataset was introduced for place recognition under time-of-day and viewpoint change [4]. The public query URL was confirmed through the dataset-formatting documentation [27]. A direct full-archive transfer exceeded the chosen bounded timeout and was not treated as a successful dataset download. Instead, the downloader read the ZIP central directory and retrieved required members with HTTP byte ranges. It checked the decompressed size and the archive’s CRC for each member before writing it. SHA256 fingerprints were then recorded for future reproduction. Partial archive files are not used as valid complete archives. All available CSV members were downloaded before subset selection. Records were grouped by their exact latitude-longitude site key. A complete selected site needed a front-facing daytime image, a left-facing daytime image, a front-facing night image and a front-facing sunset image. The first 24 complete site keys in lexicographic order were retained. That produces 96 image files with a transparent, metadata-only selection rule. Figure 5.1 illustrates the resulting condition coverage. Visual inspection confirms that the retained night examples are real night photographs rather than images created by gamma correction. It also shows that a left-facing daytime observation can depict substantially different scene content from the front-facing gallery image. This makes the day-to-day split a viewpoint stress test, not necessarily an easier control than the aligned cross-time pairs. 5.3.2 Reference-to-query direction Condition names throughout the artifact follow the arrow from reference to query. Day-to-night uses a daytime front reference and a night front query. Night-to-day reverses those roles. Day-to- sunset uses a daytime front reference and a sunset front query. Day-to-day uses a daytime front reference and a daytime left query. There is one query per selected site in each of these protocols. The gallery has one reference per selected site. Place correctness uses the stored site identity, not a distance threshold inferred after observing predictions. The reverse protocol is useful because extraction and matching may not behave symmetrically when query and reference roles change. It nevertheless reuses the same physical sites, so the protocols are related observations rather than independent geographic test sets. 5.3.3 Difference from the official benchmark The official Tokyo retrieval task uses a street-view image database. The executed protocol uses query photographs as a small cross-time reference gallery. This changes database scale, appearance distribution, viewpoint alignment and distractor difficulty. Results are therefore labelled “Tokyo 25 Chapter 5. Datasets and Data Preparation cross-time subset” throughout the thesis. They must not be compared directly with published official benchmark recall values. The restriction is scientifically important when recall saturates. A small gallery with aligned front-facing views can be easy even though night recognition is difficult in a larger operational setting. Conversely, a deliberately different viewing direction can reduce overlap despite unchanged time of day. The experiment identifies these task properties rather than treating all appearance labels as a fixed difficulty ordering. The query archive does not provide the calibrated camera poses or per-pair homographies needed for metric localisation or true planar-accuracy scoring. GPS site labels support recognition evaluation only. Geometric acceptance is reported, but a successful fitted homography is not assigned a metric translation error. The missing pose criteria are explicitly listed as unavailable in the results. 5.4 Synthetic appearance and camera perturbations 5.4.1 Source images and identity semantics The synthetic set contains transformations of both repository images and selected HPatches references. Repository filenames do not establish independent real-world places. Their labels are therefore source-image identities. Retrieving a transformed reference.jpg means recognising its source image, not proving that the system has generalised to a new geographic location. Six source images are transformed under five conditions and three fixed seeds, giving 90 generated queries. The gallery includes additional HPatches references as distractors. Every generated query has a known source identity and a known reference-to-query homography. The preparation manifest records the generated file hashes, seeds and benchmark-manifest hash so the exact test inputs can be regenerated and checked. 5.4.2 Photometric operations The daytime condition changes brightness within a bounded range. Night conditions apply a gamma curve, reduced gain and additive noise. The severe condition uses a stronger attenuation; a warm-night condition additionally changes channel gains. The fog-like condition blends a bright low-contrast component and applies mild blur. These are explicit stressors, not calibrated physical camera or weather models. Figure 5.2 provides an audit of their visual effect. The operations preserve scene geometry and do not introduce night-specific light sources, glare, moving objects or seasonal occlusion. Additive noise is not a full sensor noise model. A good result here establishes tolerance to these implemented perturbations only. Real Tokyo images provide a separate, narrower check under natural temporal appearance change. 27 Chapter 5. Datasets and Data Preparation day night night severe warm night fog day night night severe warm night fog Figure 5.2: Actual seeded synthetic queries generated from the two repository images. Columns show the evaluated photometric conditions. “Fog” denotes a contrast-and-blur simulation, not a real weather capture. 5.4.3 Known geometry and deterministic seeds Before appearance modification, a small random projective warp perturbs the image corners. The seed determines both this warp and the subsequent photometric randomness. The homography is stored explicitly, including the scale mapping from the original reference to the working-resolution source. This detail prevents a synthetic experiment from accidentally comparing an estimate in resized coordinates with a ground-truth matrix in original coordinates. The three query seeds support repeatability and sensitivity analysis. They do not create three independent physical scenes. Confidence statements must therefore preserve source identity as a grouping variable. Likewise, increasing the number of augmentations does not compensate for the small number of base photographs. The thesis reports those dependencies as validity constraints. 5.5 Training and evaluation separation The optional adaptation experiment reserves the first four illumination and first four viewpoint sequences for training the projection head. Remaining selected sequences form the held-out HPatches retrieval evaluation. Training never uses Tokyo photographs. Additional synthetic training perturbations use a separate fixed seed list. The backbone remains frozen, and no test-based checkpoint selection is performed. The main pretrained comparison may evaluate all selected HPatches sequences because none is used to train the supplied models within this artifact. The adaptation table uses only its held-out identities. Its numbers should therefore be compared with the pretrained descriptor reevaluated on that same held-out subset, not with a main-table average over a different set. The scripts preserve 28 Chapter 5. Datasets and Data Preparation both denominators to prevent that drift. 5.6 Open-set diagnostic An additional diagnostic uses HPatches images as unknown queries against a Tokyo gallery. These images have no valid place identity in that gallery. A retrieval system still returns a ranking, but an anchoring system should reject all candidates unless there is sufficient evidence. The diagnostic reports acceptance as an error condition; retrieval recall is not meaningful when no correct gallery identity exists. The collection-level difference makes this a limited open-set test. It does not represent a difficult nearby look-alike building, malicious image replay, or two nearly identical store fronts. Its purpose is to verify that the pipeline can return no anchor and to expose gross false acceptance. More realistic negative data are required before using the measured rejection behavior as a safety assurance. 5.7 Larger benchmarks not included Official Aachen, RobotCar and Extended CMU documentation and download locations were inspected. Their image and mapping archives were not downloaded for the executed comparisons. The choice reflects the already bounded laptop experiment and the additional mapping, calibration and evaluation work needed to report pose metrics correctly. They are not described as universally inaccessible or as requiring registration when the recorded sources were publicly reachable. MSLS was inspected as a route to broader seasonal and sequence coverage. Its official repository points to its current download site and describes relevant subtasks [23]. No MSLS images were included. Pittsburgh, SF-XL, Oxford/Paris and Google Landmarks were candidate alternatives rather than attempted downloads in this run. The artifact makes no statement that these untested candidates failed to download. Exact manual locations and expected layouts for the principal missing benchmarks are provided in Chapter A. 5.8 Integrity and idempotent acquisition The downloader validates both archive-derived member properties and locally recorded hashes. Repeated execution checks existing files and skips a valid collection. Missing data can be restored and checked against the pinned manifest; an existing corrupt file produces an explicit error instead of silently changing the input. Archive paths are not extracted blindly: selected basenames and sequence directories determine destinations. File-count checks enforce the expected image and homography structure. The final benchmark.json freezes protocol definitions before inference, and its hash is recorded with the run configuration. These controls do not prove that the original benchmark labels are error-free, but they establish exactly which input bytes and label rules produced the thesis results. 29 Chapter 6 Methodology 6.1 Notation and coordinate conventions An original reference image is denoted I r o and an original query I q o . Methodology The original script budgets and preprocessing remain in the separate upstream execution. The normalised comparison converts each working image to grayscale and extracts features once. Empty descriptor sets are represented explicitly. No claim is made that the common budget yields an identical number of points for the two detectors: each detector selects its own repeatable structures, and SIFT may return multiple oriented features at related locations. The recorded feature and match counts describe the realised outputs. 6.2.2 Descriptor matching For each reference descriptor d i , approximate search identifies its first and second query neighbours, e j 1 and e j 2 . The tentative correspondence survives when ∥d i − e j 1 ∥ 2 < ρ ∥d i − e j 2 ∥ 2 , (6.3) with ρ fixed in the configuration. FLANN settings match the recorded index strategy [6]. The matcher guards against fewer than two returned neighbours. Its output is a coordinate correspon- dence set, not a place decision. To extend the one-reference baseline to place recognition, Method A verifies every gallery reference. Candidates are ranked by RANSAC inlier support and then by inlier ratio, with stable order for remaining ties. The best accepted candidate supplies the anchor. A ranking is still retained when no candidate is accepted so retrieval quality and anchoring rejection can be analysed separately. 6.3 Method B: pretrained learned local matching SuperPoint supplies keypoint positions, descriptors and the feature tensors required by LightGlue [7]. The pretrained networks are loaded in evaluation mode and executed without gradient recording. The input is the same working-resolution grayscale image used by the comparison; additional internal resizing is disabled. The model is not fine-tuned in the main A–D experiment. This notation describes the role of the pretrained matcher rather than rederiving all of its layers. The official model supplies the adaptive depth and feature-pruning behavior [9]. Recorded configuration values identify the executed path. Method B is evaluated in two ways. Oracle-pair evaluation supplies the correct reference pair so local correspondence quality can be isolated. Exhaustive gallery evaluation performs learned matching against every reference, allowing retrieval and verification to be compared with Method A on identical queries. Exhaustive matching is an informative accuracy reference but may have unacceptable query cost as the gallery grows. 31 Chapter 6. The relation illustrates why descriptor ambiguity can raise geometric- estimation cost. It is a theoretical interpretation, not a claim that each recorded call used exactly this number of iterations. 6.5.3 Acceptance policy The verifier requires a minimum inlier count, a minimum inlier ratio, a finite full-rank map and an admissible projected boundary. After normalising the homogeneous scale, it rejects severe numerical conditioning, collapsed projected area and a reference boundary crossing the projective horizon. The latter is checked through denominator signs at the corners. Convexity of the projected quadrilateral supplies an additional sanity check. Homogeneous scale normalisation precedes numerical threshold checks: multiplying a valid map by a small nonzero constant must not change its validity, projected points or rendered content. Anchor polygons are independently checked for finite, ordered, convex corners. Stored normalised coordinates must lie within the reference image; crossed or collapsed polygons are rejected before warping. These conditions reduce obvious geometric failures but do not certify a correct physical anchor. A wrong repeated facade can produce a consistent planar map. A correct place can contain several depth layers that violate a single homography. A large region can project outside the visible query. Algorithm 1 Shared local verification Require: Reference/query features, reference image shape, fixed thresholds 1: Match descriptors and recover coordinate pairs (x r,j , x q,j ) 2: if fewer than four pairs exist then 3: return rejection with empty support 4: end if 5: Estimate H and an inlier mask with RANSAC 6: Count inliers and compute their fraction of tentative matches 7: Normalise H and test finiteness, rank, conditioning and boundary validity 8: return H, mask, support statistics, and the combined acceptance decision Algorithm 1 applies unchanged to the two normalised local methods. This is important for attributing an improvement to correspondence rather than to a weaker geometric acceptance rule. The implementation stores failures as rows, so a method cannot improve its reported accuracy by excluding difficult pairs from the denominator. 6.6 Method D: hierarchical recognition and anchoring The full pipeline ranks the gallery globally, selects a fixed-size shortlist, and performs Method B’s local verification on that shortlist. It selects the accepted candidate with the strongest inlier support, breaking ties by ratio. An absent accepted candidate yields no place and no rendered post. The primary configuration uses the recorded shortlist size; additional runs vary that size and remove stages. Algorithm 2 Hierarchical place and content query Require: Query I q , cached reference features, descriptor matrix Z, place database 1: Compute global query descriptor z q and a ranked candidate list 2: Compute local query features once 3: for each of the first k reference candidates do 4: Run Algorithm 1 against the cached reference features 5: Retain diagnostics and any accepted transformation 6: end for 7: if no candidate is accepted then 8: return no anchor and the candidate diagnostics 9: end if 10: Select the strongest accepted reference and its place identifier 11: Retrieve that place’s posted-content records 12: Compose content-to-reference and reference-to-query transformations 13: Render content with explicit alpha and return the verified place Algorithm 2 implements the hierarchy reviewed in Chapter 2. Global retrieval limits search, while geometry supplies the map needed by the renderer. It does not provide an independent world-scale estimate. Reference caching and one-time query extraction reduce duplicated work but 34 Chapter 6. Methodology do not remove the cost of matching several candidates. 6.6.1 A decomposition of failure Let G denote that a usable correct reference enters the shortlist, L that sufficient correct local evidence is recovered, and V that the verifier accepts an adequate map. Then the desired event is bounded by the upstream stages: P (G ∩ L ∩ V ) = P (G)P (L | G)P (V | G, L). (6.12) This is a probability identity, not an independence assumption. It explains why increasing local accuracy cannot recover a reference excluded by retrieval, and why perfect retrieval cannot ensure anchoring when the images do not overlap. The ablation tables expose these failure pathways using recorded intermediate decisions. False acceptance is a different event: a candidate may pass V without being the correct place or without satisfying ground-truth planar accuracy. Reporting only the acceptance rate would reward such failures. The results therefore pair acceptance with correctly verified identity and, where available, actual corner-error success. 6.7 Content coordinates and rendering A content asset has its own pixel domain. Let A c→r map its four corners to a normalised reference-anchor quadrilateral converted into reference pixels. The composed transform is H c→q = H r→q A c→r . (6.13) This order follows directly from applying the content-to-reference mapping first. A reversed order would generally produce an unrelated projection and is not interchangeable even though both matrices are 3 × 3. For premultiplied content colour αC and warped alpha α ′ , compositing is I out = warp(αC, H c→q ) + (1 − α ′ )I q . (6.14) An asset without an alpha channel receives an explicit opaque mask before the configured opacity is applied. This preserves black pixels as valid content. Rendering is skipped when the selected transformation is invalid or no candidate is accepted. The current application supports planar image posts; world-space occlusion and illumination-consistent three-dimensional rendering are future requirements. 35 Chapter 6.
