Exhaustive local verification repeats pair matching M times, while the hierarchy repeats it k times after retrieval. Query extraction is shared across those comparisons. These expressions describe scaling of the chosen implementation; adaptive matcher behavior and image size still determine actual measured latency. The evaluation stores individual feature and pair timings so stage costs can be inspected. Their sums are labelled stage sums, not independently timed complete queries. A separate isolated profiler executes query and rendering paths on predecoded images, with cached gallery features, to measure actual wall-clock behavior and peak process memory. Keeping these definitions separate prevents cached evaluation work from producing an implausible online throughput claim. 37 Chapter 7 Projective Geometry: Derivation and Worked Examples 7.1 Why the coordinate model deserves a separate analysis The complete Stitch query connects three image domains: the posted asset, a stored reference photograph and the visitor’s camera frame. A visually plausible result can still be geometrically wrong if any boundary uses the inverse transformation or a different resizing convention. This chapter derives those boundaries and explains the numerical checks used in the implementation. The numerical examples are algebraic illustrations, not additional benchmark measurements. The projective model follows the standard image-geometry treatment in Hartley and Zisserman [17]; the experiment remains a planar image-to-image study. A point in a photograph has two pixel coordinates. A persistent physical point would additionally require information about camera calibration and scene depth. The distinction is easy to lose because both a homography and a pose can be represented by matrices. Their dimensions, domains and observable constraints are different. Here, the output of local verification is a relation between two image planes. It cannot be interpreted as metres of displacement or as the visitor’s absolute orientation. 7.2 Homogeneous representation and scale freedom e = (u, v, 1) ⊤ . For a nonsingular 3 × 3 matrix H, the corresponding Represent an image point as x point is   a    b  = H x e ,   e ) = (a/c, b/c) ⊤ . π(H x (7.1) c Multiplying H by any nonzero scalar leaves the result unchanged wherever c ̸ = 0. Consequently, matrix entries cannot be interpreted independently of their homogeneous scale. A numerical validity check must not reject 10 −12 H while accepting H solely because its unnormalised entries 38 Chapter 7. Projective Geometry: Derivation and Worked Examples are smaller. The implementation normalises an admissible map before applying absolute denominator tolerances. For the rectangular reference domain used here, the upper-left point is included. A zero bottom-right entry maps that point onto the projective horizon and is therefore rejected by the boundary policy. This is an application-domain restriction, not a statement that every projective matrix with a zero bottom-right entry is globally meaningless. Normalisation can itself overflow if the entries span a range beyond the floating-point represen- tation. The corrected verifier checks finiteness again after division and rejects an unrepresentable map before invoking matrix decompositions. Rejection is preferable to returning an exception from an otherwise routine candidate comparison. The regression suite exercises both very small homogeneous scales and a matrix whose normalisation cannot be represented reliably. 7.3 The correspondence equations For a reference point (u, v) and query point (u ′ , v ′ ), the reference-to-query mapping implies u ′ (h 31 u + h 32 v + h 33 ) = h 11 u + h 12 v + h 13 , ′ v (h 31 u + h 32 v + h 33 ) = h 21 u + h 22 v + h 23 . (7.2) (7.3) Each correspondence therefore contributes two linear constraints on the nine homogeneous matrix entries. Four correspondences provide eight constraints, which is the minimum count for a general eight-degree-of-freedom homography when the configuration is nondegenerate. More correspondences do not automatically provide more independent information: repeated points or a nearly collinear arrangement can still leave the estimate unstable. Stitch delegates robust estimation to OpenCV rather than implementing a separate direct linear solver. The equations nevertheless explain two important rejection cases. A blank image supplies no constraints, so it must yield no map. A set of points along one edge may supply many tentative matches but insufficient two-dimensional support. An absolute inlier count cannot diagnose either case by itself; matrix and projected-boundary checks remain necessary. 7.4 Resizing as a change of coordinate system Let the original reference size be (w r , h r ) and the working size be ( w̄ r , h̄ r ). The implemented pixel transform is S r = diag( w̄ r /w r , h̄ r /h r , 1). (7.4) There is a separate transform S q for the query. If H o maps original reference coordinates to original query coordinates, the working-resolution relation is H w = S q H o S r −1 . 39 (7.5) Chapter 7. Projective Geometry: Derivation and Worked Examples e r,w into the original mapping and then applying e r = S r −1 x This equation follows by substituting x S q . It is a coordinate conversion; it does not estimate a new physical relation. Consider an illustrative reference reduced from 1000 × 800 to 500 × 400, and a query retained at its original size. An original reference point (200, 100) becomes (100, 50) in the working reference. If the original relation is a translation of (20, 10) pixels, directly applying that translation matrix to (100, 50) gives (120, 60), which is wrong for the unchanged query domain. The conjugated relation produces (220, 110), as required. The translation did not change physically; its input coordinate unit changed. Integer rounding makes horizontal and vertical scale values slightly different for some dimensions. The implementation records the realised output size rather than assuming an ideal shared scale. This matters when corner-error thresholds are only a few working pixels. A resizing approximation that is negligible to a global descriptor can still affect a geometric pass/fail boundary. 7.5 Forward and backward transfer error The reference-to-query direction is fixed throughout the prototype. A forward transfer residual for a correspondence is e r ) − x q ∥ 2 . r f = ∥π(H x (7.6) Its unit is a query pixel. A backward residual uses H −1 and has reference-pixel units. Adding the two without accounting for image scale can mix different units. A future symmetric error policy should therefore specify the coordinate systems and normalisation explicitly, rather than describing an unspecified bidirectional error as universally stricter. The reported corner metric is a different quantity. It compares the estimated and ground-truth maps at the same four reference corners. It is not the average RANSAC correspondence residual, and it can remain large when a small interior cluster fits well. This is why the report retains both local support statistics and independent corner-error success on collections that provide ground truth. On Tokyo, no independent corner relation is available for the retained cross-time pairs. Mea- suring the residual of the very correspondences used to estimate the map would not replace that missing ground truth. Such a residual could describe self-consistency, but it would not establish correct surface alignment. The site atlas consequently reports identity and decision states without inventing a Tokyo corner-error score. 7.6 RANSAC success probability and its limits In an idealised sampling calculation, let w be the probability that a tentative correspondence is a genuine inlier and let a minimal sample contain s correspondences. If samples are independent, the probability of at least one all-inlier sample after N attempts is P = 1 − (1 − w s ) N . 40 (7.7) Chapter 7. Projective Geometry: Derivation and Worked Examples Solving for a desired probability gives N ≥ log(1 − P ) . log(1 − w s ) (7.8) For a homography, s = 4 in the generic minimal case. The expression explains why a lower inlier fraction can increase robust-estimation work sharply [19]. It is an analytical sampling model, not a guarantee that a selected sample is nondegenerate or that the scene satisfies a planar relation. Repeated windows illustrate the distinction. A matcher may return many mutually consistent correspondences between different but similar structures. RANSAC can fit those correspondences and return strong support. Its success at finding a consensus does not prove the gallery identity or the physical presence of the user. The open-set diagnostic tests that broader decision problem and records wrong acceptances rather than reclassifying them as successful geometry. 7.7 The projective horizon and boundary policy The projective denominator at a reference point is the affine function d(u, v) = h 31 u + h 32 v + h 33 . On a rectangular domain, its extrema occur at vertices. If all four vertex values have the same strict sign, the denominator does not cross zero anywhere inside the rectangle. Opposite signs imply a horizon crossing and potentially unbounded image coordinates. This supplies an inexpensive domain-level validity check before rendering. The verifier also checks projected convexity and a minimum projected area. These are practical filters for a stable reference boundary. They do not establish that the entire physical scene is planar, that occluders are absent or that a target surface is safe for displaying content. A highly foreshortened but genuine target can be rejected by the area policy; the resulting loss should be counted as rejection rather than hidden by changing the denominator of an accuracy metric. A condition-number threshold serves a related numerical purpose. It identifies matrices for which inversion or perturbation may be sensitive. Its value depends on the coordinate representation, so it should be treated as an implementation policy evaluated at the recorded working resolution. It is not a universal physical plausibility score or a calibrated probability of anchor correctness. 7.8 Content coordinates and alpha compositing The asset has its own corners, which generally differ from reference-image corners. A content- to-reference map A is constructed from the asset corners and its stored reference polygon. The rendered content map is HA. The multiplication order is essential: AH applies a reference/query relation in the wrong input domain. Normalised anchor coordinates are first converted using the actual working reference width and height. An anchor polygon must contain four finite corners in a consistent boundary order and form a noncollapsed convex quadrilateral. A crossed polygon is not a harmless alternative ordering: it can induce a folded or unbounded warp. The renderer rejects that input, and database validation additionally checks that stored normalised coordinates lie in [0, 1]. Associating the polygon with a 41 Chapter 7. Projective Geometry: Derivation and Worked Examples specific photograph prevents an anchor defined on a front view from being copied onto an unrelated side view. Alpha compositing uses premultiplied colour. If the asset colour is C, its opacity mask is α, and the frame is F , the compositor evaluates the warped premultiplied colour plus F (1 − α w ). Warping unpremultiplied colour separately can mix invisible border colours into partially transparent edge pixels. Explicit alpha also preserves opaque black content, which would be lost by treating every black pixel as background. 7.9 What these derivations validate The derivations justify coordinate conjugation, transform direction, homogeneous scale handling and explicit alpha. The numerical regression tests validate concrete examples of those contracts. Neither form of validation substitutes for independent real-world alignment measurements. The HPatches corner metric provides one such measurement within its image-plane scope, while metric pose and long-term persistent-world tests remain future work. The practical outcome is a narrower and more defensible interface. A query either returns a supported reference-to-query map with an associated reference-bound post, or returns no anchor. It does not return a nominal world pose merely because a matrix was computed. This keeps subsequent deployment design aligned with the evidence the implemented estimator can actually provide. 42 Chapter 8 Experimental Setup 8.1 Recorded execution environment The experiments ran on the available Apple M2 laptop with the memory configuration recorded in results/environment.json. The software environment is a clean project-local CPython virtual environment. The initial default interpreter was unsuitable for the pinned dependency set, so the available system CPython interpreter was used. Dependency versions were installed and recorded rather than assumed from pre-existing user packages. The runtime reported neither CUDA nor an available MPS backend for these runs. All reported inference therefore uses the CPU. Both PyTorch and OpenCV are configured to use two threads in the controlled scripts. This restriction makes the workload explicit and avoids silently changing thread counts between methods. It does not establish that this is the fastest possible host configuration. The primary installed versions are listed in the environment artifact and dependency specifica- tion. The reproducibility bundle also records the official LightGlue and CosPlace code revisions and SHA256 hashes of all downloaded checkpoints. Model parameter counts and checkpoint sizes are obtained from actual loaded models and files. They are not inferred by counting the number of layers in a paper diagram. Recall@1, @5 and @10 share a query denominator and use the same ordered result list. Larger values of k are necessarily easier in these small galleries, so high Recall@10 is not interpreted as high-precision anchoring. For exhaustive local methods, the ranking uses inlier support even if the top candidate is not accepted. This permits a correct retrieval with insufficient evidence to render. For the full pipeline, shortlisted references are reranked locally and the remaining global ranking is retained as an unverified tail. Experimental Setup explicitly makes an unverified acceptance decision, allowing its false-acceptance consequences to be measured. 8.5 Matching and planar geometry metrics 8.5.1 Correspondence support For M tentative matches and N RANSAC inliers, inlier ratio is N/M when M > 0 and zero otherwise. Median inlier counts and mean ratios are computed across all evaluated positive pairs, including failures. A high ratio from a very small correspondence set is not equivalent to a well-supported surface map, which is why the verifier also requires an absolute count. Geometric acceptance rate is the fraction of pairs satisfying the configured support and validity conditions. On Tokyo it is the strongest available geometric decision metric, but it is not ground-truth alignment accuracy. On HPatches and synthetic pairs, independent ground-truth homographies make a stronger evaluation possible. 8.5.2 Corner-error success Let c 1 , . . . , c 4 be the working reference corners. Mean corner error is 4 1 X b c e i ) − π(H gt e c i ) . π( H e H = 2 4 i=1 (8.2) An oracle-pair homography success requires acceptance and e H ≤ 5 working pixels. Invalid estimates are failures. For cumulative error curves, they remain at infinite error so the curve denominator includes all queries. A conditional median over finite errors is interpreted only alongside the failure rate. End-to-end planar success additionally requires the selected place to be correct. A highly accurate homography to a wrong reference is not counted. This stricter metric measures the chain from candidate selection to anchoring, while oracle-pair success isolates local geometry when the correct reference is supplied. Their difference reveals search-stage losses. 8.6 Metric localisation criteria The requested position-and-orientation thresholds require calibrated ground-truth camera poses. For world-to-camera parameters (R, t) and (R g , t g ), the corresponding errors would be e t = −R ⊤ t + R g ⊤ t g e R = arccos clip 2 , tr(RR g ⊤ ) − 1 , −1, 1 2 (8.3) !! . (8.4) The utility function returns camera-centre distance and angle in degrees. Neither utility execution on a unit test nor GPS site metadata supplies the real query poses needed for a benchmark 46 Chapter 8. Experimental Setup measurement. The result table therefore records the three requested criteria as unavailable. Official map-based benchmarks provide the proper route for future evaluation [22]. 8.7 Timing, memory and model-size protocols The upstream measurements time bounded script execution including initialisation and file I/O. The main evaluation records feature-extraction and matching-plus-geometry times, reusing cached reference computation. Its query stage sum adds the realised query extraction and selected pair costs; it is useful for accounting but excludes some application work and is not a direct end-to-end stopwatch measurement. The separate runtime profiler starts an isolated process for each method. It builds the reference cache, warms the path, and times actual query and rendering calls on a fixed small set of predecoded Tokyo images with repeated execution. It reports median, mean and upper-tail latency, and stores every timing sample. Asset loading during rendering remains inside the measured call. Camera decoding, network transfer and display are excluded. Peak RSS is obtained from the operating system’s process resource accounting, with platform- specific units converted into bytes. It includes imports, model weights, gallery caches and transient allocation. It is not presented as the exclusive tensor memory of the selected model. Serialized model size is measured from file length and reported separately. No phone power, thermal, battery or neural-accelerator measurement is claimed. 8.8 Uncertainty and statistical interpretation For a binary site-level outcome with k successes among n sites, the report computes a Wilson interval. With p b = k/n and a normal quantile z, its centre and half-width are µ W = p b + z 2 /(2n) , 1 + z 2 /n z h W = 1 + z 2 /n s p b (1 − p b ) z 2 + 2 . n 4n (8.5) (8.6) The interval remains nonzero even when every selected query succeeds. It describes finite-sample uncertainty under an independent-site approximation, not a correction for the metadata-based geographic selection or the changed Tokyo benchmark task. HPatches uncertainty is also computed with a cluster bootstrap that samples sequence identities and includes their associated targets. Synthetic variants are discussed as repeated observations of a few sources, not independent places. For projection training, three fixed seeds yield a mean, sample standard deviation and a small-sample t interval. With so few seeds the interval is unstable; it communicates uncertainty rather than establishing a precise population effect. No significance claim is based on selecting the best seed, dropping rejected queries or treating thousands of pixel matches as independent successful places. No hyperparameters are chosen using 47 Chapter 8. Experimental Setup the test-set result tables. The design is an exploratory reproducible comparison, with the limited data coverage made explicit. 8.9 Ablations and failure inspection The shortlist-size ablation compares one, three and five candidates. Exhaustive learned matching removes the global stage, and global-only retrieval removes local geometric evidence. A no-geometry acceptance diagnostic shows the distinction between a candidate rank and a supported anchor. Projection training compares available sequence images with and without extra synthetic night variants. Export validation compares native, float ONNX and QDQ INT8 descriptors. Qualitative selections follow documented rules: prefer a case where learned local verification succeeds while SIFT rejects, otherwise use a fixed fallback. Correspondence coordinates and masks are saved by an actual rerun, and overlay figures use saved estimates. This is a deliberately illustrative selection rather than a random sample of success. Failure examples and aggregate tables prevent the selected demo from standing in for overall accuracy. 8.10 Reproducibility controls Every substantive execution command is recorded with its argument vector, working directory, start time, output-log path, elapsed time and exit code. Failed actions remain in the journal. Build scripts derive tables and figures from measured files and record input hashes. A final checker scans the PDF build log for errors and unresolved citations/references, checks data-to-table consistency, and verifies that required demonstration files can be decoded. These controls do not make future results bitwise identical across all hardware. They do make the experiment inspectable: a reader can determine the source images, exact model bytes, protocol definitions, configuration and command that produced a reported value. The appendices provide those routes without presenting an unexecuted command as an observed result. 48 Chapter 9 Decision Analysis and Statistical Interpretation 9.1 The unit of success An evaluation of Stitch can count descriptors, tentative matches, image pairs, queries, sites or user sessions. Those units answer different questions. A system may improve the number of inliers without improving the number of users who see a correctly attached post. The present evaluation makes the query the decision unit and retains site or sequence identities for interpreting dependence. Pixel correspondences provide evidence within a decision; they are not independent repetitions of the application task. This distinction also limits claims about large sample counts. The 90 synthetic queries originate from six source images. Increasing the number of seeded transformations makes the stress test more repeatable and exposes variability within those sources, but it does not add 90 independently sampled physical places. Likewise, the five HPatches targets for a sequence remain related observations of the same source. The scene atlases preserve these groupings rather than presenting every row as independent geographic coverage. 9.2 A decision tree for one query The first branch asks whether the correct place is represented in the gallery. The known-place protocols answer yes by construction, while the open-set diagnostic answers no. A retrieval ranking is meaningful in the first case. In the second, an anchoring system must decide whether to reject despite having a nearest neighbour. Every finite gallery can produce a top-ranked image; the existence of that rank does not establish a valid match. For a known query, the next branch asks whether candidate generation retains a useful reference. The full method considers only its shortlist for local verification. A correct reference outside the shortlist cannot be rescued by improving RANSAC on the candidates already selected. An exhaustive learned-local method removes that search restriction but incurs more pair comparisons. 49 Chapter 9. Decision Analysis and Statistical Interpretation The two methods therefore expose a cost–coverage tradeoff rather than an unconditional ordering in quality. The final branches distinguish rejection, wrong-place acceptance and correct-place acceptance. On collections with independent homography ground truth, correct-place acceptance is subdivided into accurate and inaccurate planar alignment. These leaves explain why retrieval recall, correctly verified-place rate and end-to-end H5 appear separately. Combining them into one unnamed accuracy number would hide the stage at which an apparent improvement occurs. 9.3 Coverage, precision and conditional denominators Let N be the number of queries, A the number of accepted decisions, C the number of correctly accepted identities and W = A − C the wrong accepted identities. Acceptance coverage is A/N , correctly verified-place rate is C/N , and accepted-identity precision is C/A when A > 0. The identity C A C = N N A (9.1) shows why a highly selective system can achieve strong conditional precision while returning few useful anchors. The report’s primary verified rate uses the full query denominator. A future application study should additionally report coverage and precision together, including an explicit convention for the no-acceptance case. On homography datasets, define G as correctly accepted queries whose corner error is within the declared tolerance. Then G/N measures the full recognition-to-alignment chain. Reporting G/C alone would answer how often an already correct accepted identity has accurate geometry. That conditional measure can be informative, but omitting C/N would conceal search and rejection failures. The atlas includes both stages so the reader can inspect this separation at sequence level. 9.4 Paired comparisons and discordant cases Two methods evaluated on the same query should be compared as paired outcomes. Partition the queries into both correct, neither correct, method A only correct and method B only correct. If the two discordant counts are n 10 and n 01 , the difference in full-denominator success rates is ∆= n 01 − n 10 . N (9.2) The two methods can have equal aggregate scores while succeeding on different images. That pattern matters operationally: combining reference coverage or improving a particular failure mode may be more useful than choosing one method globally. Each HPatches atlas entry reports learned-only and SIFT-only oracle successes for its five targets. These counts describe the observed paired evidence. They are not presented as independent significance tests for every sequence. Testing many small subsets after inspecting their results would invite selection effects, especially when the same images appear in several method comparisons 50 Chapter 9. Decision Analysis and Statistical Interpretation and ablations. The Tokyo site atlas uses an analogous paired view across conditions. A site’s changed-direction daytime query and front-facing night query share a physical identity but differ in overlap and acquisition conditions. Their comparison is valuable for diagnosing reference coverage. It does not isolate an illumination treatment because view direction is not held fixed between those two protocols. 9.5 Confidence intervals and saturated scores A score of 100 percent on 24 selected sites is a statement about those 24 decisions. It is not a proof that the system succeeds on all future night queries. The Wilson intervals in the results chapter retain finite uncertainty at the boundary. Their assumptions remain limited by the subset’s metadata-based selection and geographic coverage. A wider nominal interval cannot repair a gallery that excludes difficult scene types before evaluation. For repeated targets within HPatches sequences, a sequence-level bootstrap respects more of the grouping than resampling individual targets independently. In each bootstrap replicate, whole sequence identities are sampled and all their associated outcomes contribute. This preserves within-sequence dependence in the resampling design. It still cannot create new locations, camera models or weather conditions that were absent from the selected data. The three-seed projection experiment measures a different source of variability. Its seed standard deviation concerns the short optimisation procedure on a fixed train/test partition. It does not measure uncertainty over all possible partitions, all training collections or all urban environments. The corresponding small-sample interval is therefore interpreted as a description of this bounded adaptation exercise, with no broad claim of statistical superiority. 9.6 Selection bias and the reference gallery The gallery is part of the task definition. A small gallery of distinct scenes can make global retrieval easier than a large gallery containing adjacent views and repeated structures. Adding distractors changes the ranking problem even when the query photographs remain identical. Consequently, the custom Tokyo scores cannot be transferred to the official street-view task by changing the dataset name in a caption. The subset requires complete front/day, left/day, front/night and front/sunset observations. That rule supports controlled paired comparisons, but it selects the sites for which all required metadata combinations are available. It may exclude sites whose observations are incomplete or otherwise difficult to group. The chosen lexicographic ordering further fixes a reproducible subset without making it a random sample of the entire city. HPatches contributes independent image-to-image homographies, which strengthens the ge- ometric evaluation. Its cropped or scene-specific image pairs nevertheless differ from arbitrary visitor camera motion and world-map persistence. A successful H5 result supports the stated 51 Chapter 9. Decision Analysis and Statistical Interpretation planar relation; it does not establish performance for nonplanar scenes or for an AR session that continues after the recognised surface leaves the frame. 9.7 Threshold tuning and locked evaluation The current support and geometry thresholds are shared across the compared local methods. A future deployment may reasonably tune a decision policy, but that tuning should use a separate validation population. Selecting thresholds on the final test rows and then reporting the resulting rates as an untouched evaluation would make the apparent improvement partly a consequence of selection. A useful future protocol would reserve sites for threshold calibration, keep test sites unseen, and evaluate the entire policy at a declared operating point. Rejection costs and wrong-anchor costs should be chosen from product requirements before examining the final test outcome. The current report does not claim to have completed such a policy-calibration study. Its fixed-threshold comparison is an exploratory research baseline. 9.8 Latency as a distribution of defined work The isolated profiler records actual warm query and rendering calls. Its median and upper quantile summarise a small set of predecoded queries repeated under a fixed host configuration. Those statistics should not be interpreted as a city-scale service latency distribution. The six chosen queries and their repetitions provide evidence about this local workload; they do not include network contention, camera startup, phone thermals or concurrent users. The evaluation stage sum has an even narrower definition. It reuses measured extraction and cached pair costs to account for selected work. It is useful for comparing candidate counts, but it excludes parts of the complete application call. Mixing that sum with an end-to-end runtime from another path would produce an unfair comparison. Tables retain the distinction and state whether references, decoding and rendering are included. 9.9 A claim-to-evidence reading rule Every empirical claim should be connected to its denominator, input population, output artifact and metric definition. For example, a statement about day-to-night verified places refers to the custom Tokyo protocol, 24 selected sites, accepted identity decisions and the saved prediction rows. A statement about model size refers to produced file lengths. A statement about future native tracking is a design proposal and has no measured result in this artifact. This reading rule is especially important in an expanded report. More pages provide room for derivations, failure inspection and reproducibility records, but they do not increase the experimental population. The additional scene-level chapters reorganise existing evidence so that readers can inspect all selected cases. They do not multiply the sample size or convert a narrow observation 52 Chapter 9. Decision Analysis and Statistical Interpretation into a general benchmark claim. 53 Chapter 10 Results and Discussion 10.1 Reading the evidence The results are derived from the saved predictions, pair statistics, training records, export outputs and runtime profiles. All empirical tables and plots in this chapter are generated by scripts/generate_artifacts.py. The generation step records hashes of its input result files. Headline values in the prose use generated LaTeX macros so a rerun cannot silently leave those values inconsistent with the tables. Three outcomes are kept separate throughout. Retrieval asks whether the correct identity appears in a ranked list. Correct verification asks whether the pipeline accepts the correct identity. Planar success additionally asks whether the accepted transformation agrees with an independent ground-truth homography. A result may satisfy one outcome without satisfying the next. This distinction is especially important for Tokyo, where no true planar or metric-pose error can be computed from the downloaded metadata. 10.2 Oracle-pair local matching Table 10.1: Oracle-pair matching under shared geometry settings. Results and Discussion seasonal benchmark result, phone power measurement or city-scale service cost. The report distinguishes these absences from actual negative results such as wrong accepted places or reduced retrieval after adaptation. 10.10 Threats to validity 10.10.1 Internal validity The normalised local comparison shares preprocessing dimensions, feature budgets and geometry settings, but it cannot equalise the internal training data or detector semantics of pretrained models. Approximate descriptor search and floating-point kernels can introduce small run differences. Fixed seeds, exact model hashes and cached pair accounting reduce ambiguity, while the separate original- script runs avoid conflating the refactor with unchanged upstream behavior. Some evaluation stage timings were recorded while independent preparation tasks were also active. They are therefore treated as accounting diagnostics. The isolated complete-query profiles are the principal latency evidence. Even those profiles use a small fixed query selection and a warmed process, so they do not describe cold mobile startup or worst-case thermally constrained execution. 10.10.2 Construct validity Inlier support is not ground-truth correspondence accuracy, accepted geometry is not true alignment, and place recognition is not metric localisation. The thesis reports those constructs separately. The planar corner metric itself measures extrapolation to the reference boundary, which may penalise a locally useful surface match. That is appropriate for a full-reference overlay but should be reconsidered for a smaller user-defined anchor region. The custom Tokyo gallery changes the benchmark problem. Its perfect aligned cross-time results should be read alongside its viewpoint failures and small denominator. Synthetic night and fog labels describe transformations, not natural capture conditions. The proposed mobile architecture is not an implemented phone deployment. These boundaries are retained in captions and prose to prevent a demonstration from being used as evidence for a stronger construct. 10.10.3 External validity The selected scenes, geographic region and reference directions do not cover the intended worldwide application. There are no measured seasonal transitions, construction changes, crowds, adversarial displays or long-term map revisions. A production gallery would include many more near-duplicate structures and unknown places. Extrapolating the measured false-acceptance rate or retrieval saturation to that setting would be unjustified. 67 Chapter 10. Results and Discussion 10.10.4 Statistical conclusion validity The sample is small and correlated. Three training seeds cannot characterise the full optimisation distribution, and a larger number of synthetic pixels does not create independent physical places. Intervals are presented with their grouping assumptions, not as proof of a universal method ranking. The conclusions emphasise supported direction and failure mechanisms rather than claiming statistical superiority across all deployment conditions. 10.11 Implications for the research questions The measured evidence supports learned local matching for the selected illumination changes, while providing no uniform viewpoint advantage under the planar criterion. Global retrieval can retain aligned cross-time recognition with fewer local comparisons, but it limits success under the tested direction change. Geometry reduces indiscriminate acceptance yet still produces some wrong-place decisions. Short projection adaptation is not a reliable improvement here. The executed export establishes a practical descriptor-only deployment artifact, whose tradeoffs are examined next. 68 Chapter 11 Failure Taxonomy and Diagnostic Reasoning 11.1 Failures as different observable states A missing overlay can arise from missing input, weak retrieval, insufficient correspondences, invalid geometry or absent content. Those states require different remedies. Treating all of them as a single tracking failure makes debugging difficult and can encourage an unsafe fallback that renders a stale anchor. This chapter describes a diagnostic framework grounded in the implemented module boundaries and the saved result fields. Proposed remedies are identified as future work unless the delivered code already implements them. The key distinction is between an unsupported anchor and an incorrectly supported identity. A rejection may reduce usefulness, but it avoids assigning a post to a place without sufficient evidence under the current policy. A wrong acceptance can display plausible content at the wrong physical location. The open-set and viewpoint results show why both outcomes must remain visible in the report. 11.2 Acquisition and preprocessing failures An unreadable image fails at the decoding boundary. A camera or stream that cannot open fails before feature extraction. A video that opens but produces no decodable frame also fails explicitly in the CLI. These are operational failures, not zero-recall test queries, unless an evaluation protocol deliberately includes acquisition failure in its denominator. A subtler acquisition error occurs when a frame is valid but its coordinate metadata are wrong. Orientation changes, an unexpected crop or a mismatched resize transform can leave useful visual features while invalidating the ground-truth conversion. The current file-based experiments fix the preprocessing route and retain resize transforms. A phone implementation would need additional tests for sensor orientation, camera intrinsics and display cropping. Appearance enhancement is another boundary to monitor. Changing enhancement only for 69 Chapter 11. Failure Taxonomy and Diagnostic Reasoning cached references or only for later queries alters descriptor comparability. The global index therefore includes the supported preprocessing configuration in its identity. A future adaptive enhancement policy should be evaluated as a separate method rather than introduced silently after inspecting difficult queries. 11.3 Descriptor ambiguity and gallery coverage A global descriptor compresses an image into a vector and can discard information needed to distinguish nearby repetitive views. When the correct identity ranks outside the shortlist, local verification never sees it. The full hierarchy may then reject or accept a competing reference. This failure is different from a local matcher failing on a supplied true pair, and it cannot be diagnosed from the final inlier count alone. The Tokyo changed-direction split is particularly relevant because the reference and query can have limited shared visual content. The complete site atlas shows the retained front and left photographs alongside their ranks. Those photographs support inspection of reference coverage, but the report does not infer a numerical overlap percentage from visual judgement. A future study could annotate overlap independently and analyse it as a covariate. Adding references is a plausible remedy, yet it creates new responsibilities. More references can improve coverage while increasing storage and the number of competing hypotheses. Posts must remain tied to the view on which their polygon was defined, or be transferred through a validated relation. Simply duplicating a place ID across photographs does not make an existing polygon geometrically portable. 11.4 Insufficient or unstable local evidence Low texture, blur, darkness or strong viewpoint change can reduce the number of repeatable local features. The implementation represents empty feature sets explicitly and returns an empty match list with stable dimensions. Geometry then rejects insufficient support. This behaviour prevents an application exception from being confused with a successful query that happened to return no content. The ratio filter for SIFT and the learned assignment policy for LightGlue do not produce interchangeable correspondence populations. A larger inlier count for one method can partly reflect the number and distribution of tentative matches it supplies. The pair tables therefore include acceptance and independent corner-error success. They allow a reader to identify a case with strong support but poor alignment without treating support count as a universal quality score. Spatial concentration is an additional limitation. A dozen inliers in one small repeated region can fit a transformation that extrapolates badly to the reference boundary. The current projected- boundary checks reject some implausible maps, but they are not a calibrated coverage test. A future spatial-support rule should measure point distribution and be validated on separate data 70 Chapter 11. Failure Taxonomy and Diagnostic Reasoning before replacing the fixed comparison policy. 11.5 Consensus at the wrong identity Geometric verification tests whether tentative correspondences support a model under specified thresholds. It does not directly test the semantic uniqueness of the place. Similar facades, signs or repeated architectural motifs can generate a consistent but wrong consensus. The correct response in evaluation is to retain that outcome as wrong-place acceptance, even when the fitted transformation has many inliers. The open-set diagnostic is deliberately narrow: HPatches queries are searched against a Tokyo gallery. It establishes that unrelated-collection inputs can still trigger acceptance in some variants. It does not bound the false-acceptance rate for nearby repeated buildings, screenshots of known references or maliciously crafted inputs. Those negative populations would require their own explicitly acquired and labelled test sets. A production policy could combine geometric support with reference identity margins, multiple observations or a coarse location prior. Each addition introduces new failure modes and privacy choices. A location prior can exclude the correct place when inaccurate, and temporal confirmation can preserve a wrong identity if all frames depict the same repeated structure. These mechanisms should be assessed through whole-session error rates, not assumed to solve the identity problem by construction. 11.6 Correct identity with inaccurate alignment On HPatches and synthetic data, a query can identify the correct source yet fail the H5 criterion. Possible reasons include noisy correspondences, a biased spatial distribution or an unstable estimate. The end-to-end metric separates that case from a wrong identity and from an outright rejection. The oracle-pair table further indicates whether candidate search was responsible for losing a potentially accurate relation. On Tokyo, the equivalent alignment claim cannot be measured with the available labels. A correctly verified place is therefore not renamed a successful planar anchor. The site tables preserve that uncertainty. This is a substantive limit of the evidence rather than an omission that can be repaired by drawing a more convincing overlay. The displayed demo is selected by a documented illustrative rule. Its generated motion is applied to real still images, and actual pipeline outputs are rendered. That makes it useful for inspecting the implemented path. It remains insufficient for measuring temporal drift, recovery after occlusion or alignment under real camera translation, because those phenomena are not supplied by generated two-dimensional motion alone. 71 Chapter 11. Failure Taxonomy and Diagnostic Reasoning 11.7 Content and cache failures A verified place may have no post associated with the selected reference view. Returning an empty content list is then valid database behaviour. Copying another view’s polygon to avoid an empty result would create a geometric error. The implemented binding rule defaults a post to the place’s first reference unless an explicit reference field selects another photograph. Descriptor caches can fail more silently. A matrix can have the expected shape while containing values computed from an earlier checkpoint or different resize policy. The corrected index records a checkpoint hash, preprocessing identity, reference fingerprints and format version. It rejects incompatible or nonfinite data. The reference list and fingerprint count are checked before the matrix is used for ranking. These protections address consistency, not all forms of integrity. A service would need controlled model distribution, authenticated content changes and an atomic update policy. The local JSON/NumPy artifact is intentionally inspectable and does not claim concurrent transactional guarantees. Its failure checks should be understood as research-software contracts rather than a complete multi-user storage system. 11.8 Tracing a failure without changing the benchmark Begin with the saved query identity and protocol. Check that the image hash and configuration match the frozen run. Inspect the correct identity’s global rank, then determine whether it entered the configured shortlist.
